summary: Find the minimum number of deletions (from either end) to remove both the minimum and the maximum element.
mainInsight: Only the positions of the min and max matter. You can remove from the front, the back, or from both ends; compute the cost of each strategy and take the smallest.
canonicalApproach: Compare three strategies on the two indices

cards.answer: All from the front, all from the back, or some from each end
cards.explanation: Deletions only happen at the ends, so the set of removed elements is a prefix plus a suffix.

promptVariants: Why does the answer depend only on min_idx and max_idx?
cards.answer: Removing the min and max means the removed prefix and suffix must cover both indices. With lo = min(i, j) and hi = max(i, j): front-only cost = hi + 1, back-only cost = n - lo, both-ends cost = (lo + 1) + (n - hi). Take the minimum.
cards.explanation: Ties for min or max can use any occurrence.
One scan to find the extremes' indices.

promptVariants: Why is `min(...)` of the three correct?
cards.code:
front_only = max(min_idx, max_idx) + 1
back_only = n - min(min_idx, max_idx)
both_ends = min(min_idx, max_idx) + 1 + n - max(min_idx, max_idx)
return min(front_only, back_only, both_ends)
cards.answer: front_only deletes everything up to and including the farther index (hi + 1 elements). back_only deletes from the closer index to the end (n - lo). both_ends deletes the prefix through the earlier index and the suffix from the later index. These are the only ways to cover both indices with a prefix plus a suffix, so the minimum is optimal.
keyPoints: Prefix up to the later index
cards.explanation: Considering all three covers every possibility.

cards.explanation: The single element is both the minimum and the maximum, and deleting it takes one operation. (1: one deletion removes the only element)
